contributions.statement: Put explicit security and exposure requirements (authentication, credential and data handling, public vs internal exposure, framework versions) into every spec handed to a code-generating model, because requests that omit them produced vulnerable code in about two-thirds of outputs.
contributions.evidence: §3.2 Fig. 3(b): SC1 ambiguous requirements 66% vulnerable, every model above 56%. Figure-only results, labels from GPT-5-assisted expert review with no protocol or agreement, no functional check, dataset unreleased.
relative_to: 2607.17619 appending security requirements cut vulnerabilities 19.7-33.6 pp
2606.25195 write security requirements as executable negative tests rather than principle text

contributions.statement: Expect security guidance to flip some previously secure outputs to vulnerable when the request itself conflicts with secure practice (regression up to 19%, net gain 0.12), so re-run security checks after adding guidance rather than assuming monotonic improvement.
contributions.evidence: §3.3, SC3 only: text numbers backed by a figure, same labelling caveats, and the SC3 treatment rewrites the request.
relative_to: 2605.29737 spec and prompt edits flip generated code between secure and vulnerable

reason: The poster restates the established finding that under-specified prompts yield insecure code and that stating security requirements helps. Its numbers rest on unreleased data and an unauditable labelling protocol, and it gives no per-weakness mechanism, so nothing survives as a contribution.
